source.title: It's OK That You're Not OK
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of It's OK That You're Not OK: Meeting Grief and Loss in a Culture That Doesn't Understand by Megan Devine (2017). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright. Ideas checked against the book's table of contents and published summaries/interviews (Sounds True, Shortform, Blinkist). Several cards note where Devine challenges the 'five stages' model.

cards.title: Grief is not a problem to solve but an experience to carry
cards.body:
Megan Devine, a therapist whose partner drowned in 2009, argues that most of our ideas about grief treat it as a problem: something to fix, finish or get over. She says that is the wrong frame. Some losses cannot be made right, and grief is simply the natural response to them.

If grief is not a problem, then the goal changes. Instead of trying to make the pain go away, the work becomes finding ways to carry it, and getting the support that makes carrying it possible.
cards.apply_it: Notice when you, or someone around you, talks about grief as something to 'fix'. Try replacing that thought with 'How can this be carried?'

quiz.question: How does Devine say grief should be understood?
options: As a natural response to loss that needs to be carried, not fixed
As an illness to be cured quickly
As a test of personal strength
As a sign that something went wrong
quiz.explanation: Devine argues grief is a natural response to loss; the aim is to carry it with support, not solve it.

cards.title: Being 'not OK' after a terrible loss is a sane response
cards.body:
The book's title is its core message. Devine says that when something devastating happens, being deeply unhappy, confused or broken-hearted is not a malfunction. It is what love looks like when someone is gone.

She finds that grieving people are often made to feel they are doing it wrong: too sad, too long, too openly. Her message to them is that their reaction makes sense. Removing that extra layer of self-judgement does not end the pain, but it can make it easier to bear.
cards.apply_it: If you are grieving, say to yourself today: 'It makes sense that I feel this way.' If someone else is, say it to them.

quiz.question: What is the main message behind the book's title?
options: You should be OK by now
Being not OK after a big loss is a reasonable, sane response
Being sad is a choice
Grief is mostly imagined
quiz.explanation: Devine argues intense pain after loss is a normal response, not a sign you're grieving wrongly.

cards.title: The five stages were never meant as a map for grievers
cards.body:
Devine challenges the popular 'five stages of grief'. She points out that Elisabeth Kübler-Ross first described these stages from her work with dying patients facing their own deaths, not with people mourning someone else. Over time they were turned into a neat, step-by-step path for all grief.

Devine argues that real grief is far messier: feelings arrive together, repeat and return years later. Treating the stages as a checklist can make grievers feel they are failing when their experience doesn't fit.
cards.apply_it: If you have used the five stages to judge your own grief, ask: what am I actually feeling today, without a label?

quiz.question: What is Devine's main objection to the 'five stages of grief'?
options: They are too short
They ignore anger completely
They came from dying patients and are misused as a linear checklist for grievers
They were invented recently
quiz.explanation: The stages came from Kübler-Ross's work with the dying and are wrongly treated as an orderly path all grievers must follow.

cards.title: Grief models become harmful when used to judge people
cards.body:
A second problem Devine sees with stage models is how they are used. Friends, and sometimes professionals, may say a grieving person is 'stuck in anger' or 'in denial', as if there were a correct next step they are failing to take.

Devine argues that grief has no correct sequence and no finish line. Labelling someone's grief as behind schedule adds shame to pain. A better question than 'what stage are they in?' is 'what do they need right now?'
cards.apply_it: Next time you're tempted to say someone is 'stuck', ask them instead: 'What would help you most this week?'

quiz.question: According to Devine, what question is more useful than 'What stage are they in?'
options: 'When will they be over it?'
'Why aren't they at acceptance yet?'
'Who is to blame?'
'What do they need right now?'
quiz.explanation: Devine moves the focus from judging progress to understanding what the grieving person needs.

cards.title: You don't move on from a great loss; you move forward with it
cards.body:
Many people expect grief to end after a set time. Devine disagrees with the idea of a deadline. She suggests that big losses become part of who you are. The sharpest pain usually changes with time, but you do not return to the person you were before.

Rather than 'moving on', she talks about building a life that has room for the loss. This can be a relief: it means you are not failing if you still miss someone years later.
cards.apply_it: Think of a loss from long ago that still matters to you. Instead of asking why it isn't 'over', ask how it has become part of your life.

quiz.question: How does Devine view the idea of 'moving on' after a major loss?
options: You move forward with the loss rather than leaving it behind
It is the goal of all grief
It should happen within a year
It means forgetting the person
quiz.explanation: Devine argues grief doesn't end on a schedule; you build a life that includes the loss.

cards.title: Beware the 'at least' in words of comfort
cards.body:
Devine describes how comforting sentences often go wrong in their second half. 'I'm so sorry, at least he isn't suffering.' 'It's awful, but at least you're young.' The first part acknowledges the pain; the 'at least' part quietly argues with it.

She explains that grieving people hear the second half as 'your pain is smaller than you think'. Even with good intentions, it leaves them feeling unheard. Often the kindest thing is to stop after the first half: I'm so sorry.
cards.apply_it: Before comforting someone, notice whether your sentence contains 'at least' or 'but'. Try stopping before it.

quiz.question: Why do sentences with 'at least' often hurt grieving people?
options: They are too short
They make the pain seem smaller and argue with the person's grief
They mention the person who died
They sound too formal
quiz.explanation: The 'at least' second half minimises the loss, so the person feels unheard.

cards.title: 'Everything happens for a reason' can deepen the hurt
cards.body:
Devine is critical of familiar sayings like 'everything happens for a reason' or 'they're in a better place'. Whatever your beliefs, she points out that these phrases are usually offered to close the conversation, not to stay in it. They can suggest that a death was necessary or deserved.

People may draw deep comfort from their own faith; that is theirs to choose. What hurts is having someone else's explanation pressed on you. Devine suggests offering presence rather than reasons.
cards.apply_it: Replace one go-to phrase you use around loss with something simpler, such as 'I'm here, and I'm so sorry.'

quiz.question: According to Devine, what is the problem with saying 'everything happens for a reason' to a griever?
options: It is too religious
It is too long
It can imply the loss was necessary and shuts down the conversation
It makes the speaker look weak
quiz.explanation: Such sayings often close the conversation and can imply the loss was meant to be.

cards.title: Many cultures are uncomfortable with pain, and grievers pay for it
cards.body:
Devine argues that her own society is 'emotionally illiterate' about grief. People are taught to cheer each other up, look on the bright side and stay positive, so they don't know what to do with pain that cannot be cheered away.

The result is that grieving people feel pressure to hide their feelings, or to perform recovery to keep others comfortable. Every culture has its own customs around death; Devine's point is that support works best when it makes room for pain instead of rushing it.
cards.apply_it: Think about how people in your family or community respond to grief. What helps? What pushes pain out of sight?

quiz.question: What does Devine mean by a culture being 'emotionally illiterate' about grief?
options: It doesn't have words for death
It talks about grief too much
It has no mourning rituals at all
It pushes positivity and doesn't know how to stay with pain
quiz.explanation: Devine argues a culture focused on cheering people up leaves grievers pressured to hide pain.

cards.title: Loss is not a punishment for thinking the wrong thoughts
cards.body:
Devine pushes back on what she calls a culture of blame: the idea that if you were positive enough, healthy enough or spiritual enough, bad things would not happen, and that if they do, you must have attracted them or failed to learn a lesson.

She argues this view mostly protects the speaker from the fear that loss could happen to them. For the grieving person, it adds guilt to heartbreak. Terrible things happen to good, careful, loving people, and that is not their fault.
cards.apply_it: If you catch yourself thinking a loss happened because someone 'did something wrong', ask whether that thought is really about your own fear.

quiz.question: Why, according to Devine, do people sometimes blame grievers for their loss?
options: Because it helps them feel safe from the same loss
Because it is usually true
Because grievers ask for it
Because blame speeds up healing
quiz.explanation: Blame lets people believe loss can't happen to them, but it adds guilt to the griever's pain.

cards.title: Comparing losses helps no one
cards.body:
Devine warns against comparing griefs, whether it is 'my loss is worse than yours' or 'others have it harder, so I shouldn't complain'. Every loss is real, and different losses carry different kinds of pain and long-term impact.

Comparison usually leaves someone feeling dismissed. Instead of measuring, she encourages simply honouring each person's loss for what it is. You can feel compassion for others' pain without shrinking your own, and recognise your own pain without competing.
cards.apply_it: If you have told yourself your grief 'doesn't count' because others have it worse, allow it to count today.

quiz.question: What does Devine say about comparing different people's losses?
options: Bigger losses deserve more support
Comparison usually hurts; each loss deserves to be honoured on its own terms
Comparison helps people feel grateful
Only deaths count as real losses
quiz.explanation: Losses differ, but comparing them tends to dismiss someone's pain.

cards.title: What grieving people need most is to be heard
cards.body:
A thread through the whole book is acknowledgement. Devine argues that when pain cannot be fixed, the most healing thing is to have it seen and named by another person, without them trying to talk you out of it.

She calls this being witnessed. A friend who says 'this is awful, and I'm here' often helps more than one with a page of advice. Being heard does not take the loss away, but it eases the loneliness that makes grief so much heavier.
cards.apply_it: Next time someone shares a painful thing, reflect it back ('That sounds so hard') before saying anything else.

quiz.question: What does Devine see as the most helpful response to pain that can't be fixed?
options: Giving clear advice
Changing the subject
Acknowledging and witnessing it
Reminding them of the positives
quiz.explanation: When pain cannot be fixed, being acknowledged and witnessed is what helps most.

cards.title: You can't remove the pain of loss, but you can reduce suffering
cards.body:
Devine makes a key distinction. The pain of losing someone is real and cannot be taken away. Suffering is the extra weight piled on top: harsh self-judgement, other people's careless comments, isolation, and not getting food, sleep or rest.

She argues that while the pain has to be carried, much suffering can be eased. That gives grieving people something they can actually do, without pretending the loss is fine.
cards.apply_it: List one thing adding to your suffering, such as a harsh inner voice or a draining person, and one small step to ease it this week.

quiz.question: In Devine's distinction, what is 'suffering'?
options: The loss itself
The love you had for the person
Something that can never change
The extra weight added on top of pain, like self-blame or lack of care
quiz.explanation: Pain is the loss itself; suffering is what is added to it, and much of it can be reduced.

cards.title: In early grief, just getting through the day is enough
cards.body:
In the first raw period after a loss, Devine encourages people to lower their expectations of themselves a long way. Getting out of bed, drinking water, eating something and making it to evening may be all you can do, and that is enough.

She suggests breaking time into small pieces, such as the next hour or the next task, rather than facing the whole future at once. Living in the reality of loss is exhausting, and survival is a real achievement.
cards.apply_it: If today feels too much, choose just the next hour. What is one small thing that would help you get through it?

quiz.question: What does Devine suggest about expectations in early grief?
options: Lower them and focus on getting through small pieces of time
Return to full productivity quickly
Plan the next five years
Avoid all rest
quiz.explanation: In early grief, survival is an achievement; breaking time into small pieces helps.

cards.title: Wishing not to be here is common in grief; tell someone
cards.body:
Devine writes openly about the wish many grieving people have not to be alive, often a longing to be with the person who died or simply for the pain to stop. She treats this as something to talk about honestly rather than hide.

She also encourages finding reasons, however small, to stay, and reaching out for support. If you ever have thoughts of ending your life or a plan to do so, contact a crisis line, emergency services or a doctor straight away. You deserve support, not silence.
cards.apply_it: Save a crisis line for your country in your phone now. If these thoughts come, call it or tell someone you trust the same day.

quiz.question: What does Devine recommend about the wish not to be alive during grief?
options: Keep it hidden so others don't worry
Talk about it honestly and reach out for support
Ignore it until it goes
Treat it as a sign grief is ending
quiz.explanation: Devine treats these feelings as common and important to share; anyone with thoughts of suicide should get help immediately.

cards.title: Grief can scramble memory and focus; you're not losing your mind
cards.body:
Devine describes how grief affects the mind: forgetting simple things, losing track of conversations, being unable to read a page, mixing up appointments. Many grieving people fear they are going mad.

She reassures readers that these are common effects of grief and the stress that comes with it. The brain is working hard to absorb a huge change. Knowing this is normal can ease the worry, and leaves energy for gentle workarounds.
cards.apply_it: If grief is affecting your memory, start one simple list on paper or your phone for things you must not forget this week.

quiz.question: How does Devine explain the memory and concentration problems many grievers notice?
options: They mean the person is going mad
They are caused by laziness
They are common effects of grief and stress
They only affect older people
quiz.explanation: Forgetfulness and poor focus are common effects of grief, not signs of madness.

cards.title: Make life easier for your grieving brain
cards.body:
Because grief affects memory and energy, Devine suggests reducing the load. Write things down. Use reminders. Let others help with tasks that need sharp attention, such as paperwork. Put off big decisions that can wait.

This is not giving up; it is adapting to what is true for now. She treats basic care, such as eating, resting and moving a little, as practical support for a mind and body under heavy strain, rather than as luxury or a sign of 'moving on'.
cards.apply_it: Choose one task this week that needs focus and ask someone to help you with it or do it alongside you.

quiz.question: Which approach does Devine suggest for grief's effects on the mind?
options: Push harder and take on more
Make big life decisions quickly
Ignore basic needs until the grief passes
Reduce the load with notes, reminders and help from others
quiz.explanation: Workarounds like notes and shared tasks support a mind under strain.

cards.title: After a loss, the world can feel unsafe: that anxiety makes sense
cards.body:
Devine notes that anxiety often follows a loss. Once something terrible has happened, the mind knows it can happen again, so it starts scanning for danger: worrying when someone is late, imagining the worst, checking on loved ones.

She explains that this is the mind trying to protect you, and that arguing with it logically rarely works. Seeing anxiety as an understandable reaction, rather than a personal failing, is a first step to calming it.
cards.apply_it: When an anxious 'what if' arrives, name it: 'This is my mind trying to keep me safe after a loss.'

quiz.question: Why does Devine say anxiety is common after a loss?
options: The mind has learned that terrible things can happen and scans for danger
Grievers are naturally weak
Anxiety means grief is over
It is caused by not thinking positively
quiz.explanation: A loss shows the mind that bad things happen, so it becomes watchful; that anxiety is understandable.

cards.title: When logic can't calm anxiety, start with your body
cards.body:
Devine's approach to grief-related anxiety is to work through the body when the thinking mind won't listen. Instead of debating each fear, she suggests steadying yourself physically: slowing your breath, making your out-breath longer than your in-breath, and noticing what is actually around you.

Taking care of sleep, food and rest also matters, since a tired body tends to run more anxious. If anxiety stays high or stops you living your life, talk to a health professional.
cards.apply_it: Try this now: breathe in for a count of four, then out for a count of six. Repeat five times.

quiz.question: What does Devine suggest when anxious thoughts won't respond to logic?
options: Argue harder with each fear
Calm the body, for example with slower breathing
Stay awake to keep watch
Avoid all reminders forever
quiz.explanation: Working through the body, such as with a longer out-breath, can calm anxiety when reasoning fails.

cards.title: Writing can help you tell the truth about your grief
cards.body:
Devine includes writing exercises throughout the book. She sees writing not as a way to fix grief but as a place to tell the truth about it: what happened, what it is like now, what nobody else wants to hear.

Putting things on paper can release some of their pressure and help you notice what you need. No one else has to read it, and it doesn't need to be well written. It is a private place where your grief is allowed to be exactly as it is.
cards.apply_it: Set a timer for ten minutes and write freely, starting with: 'What I wish people understood about my loss is...'

quiz.question: How does Devine see the purpose of writing in grief?
options: To produce a polished story to share
To prove you have healed
To tell the truth about your grief, not to fix it
To replace talking to others
quiz.explanation: Writing is a place for honesty about grief, not a cure or a performance.

cards.title: Creative expression keeps you company in grief
cards.body:
In a chapter on art, Devine argues that creative work, whether drawing, music, photography, crafts or writing, can be a companion to grief. Art can hold feelings that ordinary words can't, and it can be a way to stay connected to the person who died.

The point is not to produce something beautiful or turn pain into a masterpiece. It is to give your grief a form and somewhere to go. Many cultures do this already through songs, dances, cloth and memorials.
cards.apply_it: Make one small creative thing about your loss today: a drawing, a song, a photo or a collage. It doesn't have to be good.

quiz.question: Why does Devine encourage creative expression in grief?
options: To make money from the experience
To create a masterpiece
To distract from feelings completely
To give grief a form and stay connected, not to make something perfect
quiz.explanation: Art can hold what words can't and keep connection with the person, regardless of quality.

cards.title: Define what 'recovery' means for you
cards.body:
Devine questions the usual picture of recovery, which means going back to normal as if the loss never happened. She invites grieving people to find their own image of what living well alongside the loss might look like.

For one person that might be being able to laugh again while still missing someone; for another, honouring the person through their work or faith. Recovery on your own terms recognises that you are changed, and lets you decide what a good life looks like now.
cards.apply_it: Finish this sentence: 'Living well with my loss would look like...' Write down one image that comes to mind.

quiz.question: How does Devine reframe 'recovery' from grief?
options: Finding your own image of living well alongside the loss
Returning to exactly who you were
Forgetting the person who died
Following a fixed programme
quiz.explanation: Instead of returning to normal, she invites people to define their own picture of living with loss.

cards.title: You don't have to grow from loss for your grief to be valid
cards.body:
Devine resists the pressure to find a silver lining. Grieving people are often told their loss will make them stronger, wiser or more grateful, as if it were a lesson. She argues a death is not a lesson someone needed to learn.

Some people do find new meaning or purpose after a loss, and that is real. But it is not required, and it does not make the loss worth it. Grief is valid whether or not it ever turns into growth.
cards.apply_it: If someone has told you your loss will make you stronger, remind yourself: 'Any growth is mine to find or not. My grief is valid either way.'

quiz.question: What is Devine's view on 'growing' from loss?
options: Growth is the purpose of every loss
Growth may happen but is not required, and doesn't justify the loss
People who don't grow are grieving wrongly
Growth must happen within a year
quiz.explanation: She rejects the idea that loss is a lesson; any growth is optional and doesn't make the loss worth it.

cards.title: Decide when to explain your grief, and when to let it go
cards.body:
Grieving people hear a lot of unhelpful comments. Devine discusses a practical choice: should you educate the people around you about grief, or ignore them?

She suggests it depends on the relationship and your energy. People who matter to you and seem open may be worth a gentle explanation of what helps and what hurts. With others, it may be wiser to protect your energy and let the comment pass. Both choices are legitimate; you don't owe everyone an education.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone whose comments about your loss have hurt. Decide: is this a person to talk to, or a person to let go of for now?

quiz.question: What does Devine suggest about responding to unhelpful comments?
options: Always correct everyone
Never say anything
Choose based on the relationship and your energy
Cut off all friends who say the wrong thing
quiz.explanation: Whether to educate or ignore depends on how much the relationship matters and your energy.

cards.title: Help people help you by being specific
cards.body:
Devine notes that many friends want to help but don't know how, and 'let me know if you need anything' leaves the work with the grieving person. She encourages grievers, when they can, to give clear, specific requests: bring dinner on Tuesday, sit with me on Sunday, handle these calls.

She also suggests having one trusted person pass on updates and coordinate offers, so you don't have to repeat the same news again and again.
cards.apply_it: Write a short list of three concrete things that would help you, or someone you know who is grieving. Share one with a friend who offered help.

quiz.question: What does Devine suggest grieving people do when friends offer help?
options: Say they are fine
Wait for friends to guess
Refuse all help
Give clear, specific requests and let a trusted person coordinate
quiz.explanation: Specific requests, and a trusted person to coordinate, make it easier for others to help.

cards.title: Grief changes friendships: some fade, some surprise you
cards.body:
Devine acknowledges a painful side of grief: some friends disappear, unsure what to say, while others say hurtful things. At the same time, people you didn't expect, such as an acquaintance or a neighbour, may show up with real care.

She encourages grieving people not to blame themselves for these shifts. They often reflect other people's discomfort with loss. Noticing who truly supports you lets you lean on them, and grieve the friendships that changed without losing hope in people.
cards.apply_it: Name one person who has shown up for you unexpectedly during a hard time. Thank them this week.

quiz.question: How does Devine explain friends who disappear after a loss?
options: It often reflects their own discomfort with loss
The griever pushed them away
They never cared at all
It is a sign grief is over
quiz.explanation: Friends' absence often reflects their own discomfort with grief, not the griever's fault.

cards.title: Find your 'tribe of after': others who know loss
cards.body:
Devine uses the phrase 'tribe of after' for the people you meet who have also been through deep loss. They understand without needing explanations, and with them you can speak honestly.

She sees this companionship as one of the most important supports for the long road of grief. It might be a bereavement group, an online community, people in your faith community who lost someone, or one friend who has walked a similar path. Being among people who get it makes grief less lonely.
cards.apply_it: Look up one bereavement group, in person or online, or reconnect with someone you know who has also experienced a loss.

quiz.question: What does Devine mean by the 'tribe of after'?
options: Your relatives before the loss
People who have also experienced deep loss and understand it
Professionals who treat grief
People who avoid talking about death
quiz.explanation: It's the community of others who have lived through loss and understand without explanation.

cards.title: True hope doesn't ask you to pretend
cards.body:
Devine distinguishes the forced optimism grieving people are often pushed towards, with its insistence that everything will be fine and that they should look on the bright side, from a more honest kind of hope.

The hope she values sits alongside the truth of loss. It doesn't promise the pain will vanish or that things happened for the best. It grows from companionship, from small moments of connection and beauty, and from finding a way to live that honours both your love and your grief.
cards.apply_it: Name one small thing that gave you a moment of comfort this week, without needing it to cancel out the sadness.

quiz.question: What kind of hope does Devine value?
options: Insisting everything happens for the best
Hope that the pain will disappear quickly
Hope that sits honestly alongside the loss
Hiding sadness to stay positive
quiz.explanation: She values honest hope that coexists with grief rather than forced positivity.

cards.title: Love outlasts loss
cards.body:
Devine ends with the idea that love is what remains. The relationship with the person who died does not simply stop; you keep loving them, and that love shapes how you live afterwards.

In many cultures, this continuing bond is honoured openly, through remembrance days, prayers, naming children after loved ones or telling their stories. Devine suggests that, rather than trying to shut grief away, you can carry that love forward. Grief and love are closely tied: you grieve because you loved.
cards.apply_it: Do one thing this week that honours someone you have lost, such as cooking their favourite dish, telling their story or visiting a meaningful place.

quiz.question: What does Devine say remains after loss?
options: Nothing; it is best to forget
Only regret
Anger that never changes
Love for the person, which can be carried forward
quiz.explanation: She argues love lasts, and carrying it forward is part of living with loss.

cards.title: How to help a grieving friend: show up, listen, don't fix
cards.body:
The book ends with practical guidance for friends and family. Devine's advice centres on presence: show up, listen without trying to fix, and let the grieving person's feelings be as big as they are.

She encourages acknowledging the loss openly instead of avoiding it, offering concrete help rather than vague offers, and not making the conversation about your own experience. It's fine to admit you don't know what to say; staying is what matters.
cards.apply_it: Send a message to someone who is grieving: 'I'm thinking of you and of [their person]. I'd like to bring you a meal on [day]. Is that OK?'

quiz.question: Which approach fits Devine's advice on helping a grieving friend?
options: Show up, listen and offer concrete help
Tell them about your own similar loss
Offer a list of ways to feel better
Avoid mentioning the person who died
quiz.explanation: Presence, listening and concrete help matter more than having the right words or solutions.

cards.title: It's OK not to know what to say, as long as you stay
cards.body:
Devine observes that fear of saying the wrong thing leads many people to say nothing and stay away, which grieving people often experience as abandonment.

She suggests being honest about the awkwardness instead. Something like 'I don't know what to say, but I'm here' is far better than silence. Tolerating your own helplessness, without rushing to cheer someone up, is part of the support. The goal is not to find perfect words but to keep showing up.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you have avoided since their loss. Reach out with a short, honest message today.

quiz.question: What does Devine say about not knowing what to say to a grieving person?
options: Stay away until you find the right words
Admit it honestly and stay present
Send a card and say nothing more
Change the subject quickly
quiz.explanation: Admitting you don't know what to say, and staying, is better than silence or avoidance.
